scenes.heading: Acids and bases
scenes.sub: From lemon juice to drain cleaner
scenes.say: Lemon juice, vinegar, soap, drain cleaner, even your stomach. Acids and bases are everywhere. Let's find out how they behave.

scenes.heading: What are they?
points: Acid: makes H⁺ ions in water
Base: reacts with and neutralises an acid
Alkali: a base that dissolves, making OH⁻
scenes.say: An acid makes hydrogen ions, H plus, when it dissolves in water. A base is anything that reacts with an acid and neutralises it. A base that dissolves in water is called an alkali, and it makes hydroxide ions, O H minus. Remember BRA: blue litmus turns red in acid.
scenes.caption: An acid makes hydrogen ions, H⁺, when it dissolves in water. A base reacts with an acid and neutralises it. A base that dissolves in water is an alkali, and it makes hydroxide ions, OH⁻. Remember BRA: Blue litmus turns Red in Acid.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Earthquake scales go up in big jumps
scenes.science: Each pH unit is a ten-fold change in H⁺
scenes.breaks: On the pH scale a LOWER number means more acidic – backwards compared with an earthquake scale.
scenes.say: Think of the earthquake scale. It goes up in big jumps, and so does pH. Below seven is acidic, seven is neutral, and above seven is basic. Each step of one pH unit is a ten-fold change in hydrogen ions. But careful: on the pH scale, a lower number means more acidic.
scenes.caption: Think of the earthquake scale. It goes up in big jumps, and so does pH. Below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, and above 7 is basic. Each pH unit is a ten-fold change in H⁺. But careful: on the pH scale, a lower number means more acidic.

scenes.heading: Comparing pH values
scenes.question: Solution X has pH 2 and solution Y has pH 5. How many times greater is the H⁺ concentration in X?
lines: Each unit is a factor of 10
X has 1000 times the H⁺ of Y
scenes.say: Solution X has pH two, and solution Y has pH five. The difference is three pH units. Each unit is a factor of ten, so ten times ten times ten gives one thousand. X has a thousand times the hydrogen ions of Y.
scenes.caption: Solution X has pH 2 and Y has pH 5. The difference is 3 pH units. Each unit is a factor of 10, so 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000. X has 1000 times the H⁺ of Y.

scenes.heading: Neutralisation
scenes.say: When an acid meets a base, you get neutralisation. Acid plus base gives salt plus water. What really happens is each H plus pairs up with an O H minus to make water, like dance partners. The leftover ions make the salt. And the mixture warms up, because it's exothermic.
scenes.caption: When an acid meets a base, you get neutralisation. Acid + base → salt + water. Each H⁺ pairs up with an OH⁻ to make water, like dance partners. The leftover ions make the salt. And the mixture warms up, because it's exothermic.

scenes.heading: Metals vs carbonates
scenes.say: Acids also react with metals and carbonates. Metal plus acid gives salt plus hydrogen: that's MASH. Hydrogen makes a squeaky pop with a lit splint. Acid plus a carbonate gives salt, water and carbon dioxide. That's three products, so don't forget the water. Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky.

scenes.heading: Strong is not concentrated

left.title: Strong
points: How fully the acid splits into ions

right.title: Concentrated
points: How much acid is in the water
Like lots of cordial in a glass
A strong acid can still be dilute

scenes.say: Strong and concentrated mean different things. Strong is how fully an acid splits into ions. Hydrochloric acid is strong, vinegar's ethanoic acid is weak. Concentrated is how much acid is in the water, like how much cordial you pour in a glass. So you can have a dilute strong acid.

points: Acids make H⁺; alkalis make OH⁻
MASH, and carbonates give CO₂ too
scenes.say: Quick recap. Acids make H plus, alkalis make O H minus. Below pH seven is acidic, and each unit is a ten-fold change. Acid plus base gives salt and water. Metals give hydrogen, carbonates give carbon dioxide. Now try the practice questions!
